sv_cgiab/cnv_with_bed_track.note: BAF added, and the coverage lane fixed so it can be read. Both halves of the note. (1) THE BAF TRACK: chr5 is the chromosome that most rewards one -- the benchmark calls three allelic states on it where chr3 (cnv_depth_baf) has two. Measured off the hosted bigWig per 2 Mb of het sites: chr5:20-22 Mb CN 2 (1|1) is 84% between 0.4 and 0.6, chr5:37-39 Mb CN 3 (2|1) is 45% at 0.15-0.4 and 49% at 0.6-0.85, chr5:60-62 Mb CN 1 (0|1) is 48% below 0.15 and 51% above 0.85 with nothing between. So the lane draws one band, then the 1/3-2/3 fork the tutorial's own table predicts for a gain, then the two LOH bands. (2) NORMALIZED READ DEPTH, and the tool that does it: that is what the coverage lane already was -- goleft indexcov normalizes each sample to its own median, which is the only reason the two rows can be read against each other. It did not LOOK like it because the display was on localsd autoscale while the walkthrough text tells the reader to apply a manual min/max cap: indexcov's centromere and repeat spikes run to 497, so every plateau sat in the bottom fifth of the lane as one cloud. Fixed 0..3 with crosshatches now, where the tumor's three levels (0.6 / 1.1 / 1.9 by median) step against the normal's flat 1.0. Caption and the walkthrough paragraph updated; viewport 690 -> 830.

sv_cgiab/driver_kras_gain.name: sv_cgiab/driver_kras_gain
sv_cgiab/driver_kras_gain.note: DONE, and with a published pipeline rather than a homegrown one. C-GIAB hosts the New York Genome Center's somatic pipeline run on this exact HG008-T/HG008-N pair, whose BIC-seq2 output is one log2 tumour-versus-normal copy ratio per segment: 196 segments genome-wide, so it loads as a 6 KB bedGraph. Both the normalization and the segmentation are theirs. Every figure gets it as its top lane, above the depth it summarizes, and the steps land where the benchmark says: chr3 p-to-q and chr18 over SMAD4 each move a full log2 unit (CN 1 to CN 2), and the KRAS tandem duplication sits log2(3/2) above its flanks with its edges on the called boundaries. Fixed range on all four so a step means the same thing from one figure to the next, which autoscale cannot do here because a homozygous deletion has no finite ratio and one such segment flattens a whole chromosome. Shown as published, not re-centred: BIC-seq2 normalizes on total read counts and HG008-T is hypodiploid, so the balanced baseline sits above zero. The recipe is in the tutorial and in scripts/build_sv_visualization_cgiab.sh (a 20 KB download and one awk).

sv_cgiab/cnv_depth_baf.name: sv_cgiab/cnv_depth_baf
sv_cgiab/cnv_depth_baf.note: DONE, and with a published pipeline rather than a homegrown one. C-GIAB hosts the New York Genome Center's somatic pipeline run on this exact HG008-T/HG008-N pair, whose BIC-seq2 output is one log2 tumour-versus-normal copy ratio per segment: 196 segments genome-wide, so it loads as a 6 KB bedGraph. Both the normalization and the segmentation are theirs. Every figure gets it as its top lane, above the depth it summarizes, and the steps land where the benchmark says: chr3 p-to-q and chr18 over SMAD4 each move a full log2 unit (CN 1 to CN 2), and the KRAS tandem duplication sits log2(3/2) above its flanks with its edges on the called boundaries. Fixed range on all four so a step means the same thing from one figure to the next, which autoscale cannot do here because a homozygous deletion has no finite ratio and one such segment flattens a whole chromosome. Shown as published, not re-centred: BIC-seq2 normalizes on total read counts and HG008-T is hypodiploid, so the balanced baseline sits above zero. The recipe is in the tutorial and in scripts/build_sv_visualization_cgiab.sh (a 20 KB download and one awk). FOLLOW-UP: the lane now covers the whole tutorial rather than the four figures this review round named. sv_cgiab/cnv_with_bed_track (whole chr5) leads with it over the indexcov scatter, and sv_cgiab/driver_cdkn2a_deletion gained what turned out to be its strongest evidence: BIC-seq2 segments the focal homozygous deletion at chr9:21,952,524-21,972,302, the benchmark SV_75 interval to within a few dozen bp, so the segment edges, the tumour coverage cliff, the read drop-out and the CN 0 call are four independent lanes on the same two breakpoints. The track is also in demos/cgiab/config.json now and deployed, so it is available to anyone opening the demo rather than only to figures that declare it as a session track.

At ~90 My every gap is a gap and none of them is attributable to anything, so the figure moved to hg38 vs CHIMP (panTro6), which the hub already carries as hg38_to_panTro6_liftOver, at an FTO intron. WHY THAT LOCUS, measured rather than picked. hg38 chr16:54,042,096-54,048,145 is a 6,049 bp L1HS -- the youngest, still-active human LINE-1 subfamily, so human-specific by subfamily -- read out of the hub's own rmsk.bed.gz, with 641 bp of unique sequence to the nearest upstream element (THE1D) and ~4.5 kb to the nearest downstream one (AluSx). Two thirds of the genes in this window carry no 'gene' attribute at all, only a locus tag, so randomColor(undefined) painted every one of them the same strong magenta - most of the frame was one color, and it read as a large named group. Those are grey now, so a color in the figure means what the section says it means: an ortholog symbol, the same color down all three panels. This figure documents what the 'Color by attribute' dialog writes (ColorByAttributeDialog builds this exact jexl), so a hand-picked palette would be a picture of something the dialog cannot produce; and randomColor's hash was chosen over a cat10-style fixed palette on measurement - prettier at six values, collides badly past ten - for a function that also colors BAM tag values and consequence terms. If you want the fixed palette anyway, that is a core change to randomColor plus its test, not a spec edit; say the word. PALETTE NOW DONE, in randomColor itself rather than in this spec. The complaint was right and the diagnosis was that it reads as random RGB — which it literally was: the hash mapped straight into HSL, whose hue wheel spends a quarter of itself on greens that look identical and a sliver on yellow, and which at one nominal lightness gives glaring yellows beside murky blues. That unevenness is the whole difference between a hash palette and a curated one. It now places the same hash's hue in OKLCH at a fixed lightness and chroma (three tiers, 0.56/0.66/0.75 L), gamut-mapped by reducing chroma at constant hue rather than by clipping a channel, and returns hex. Every value now comes out equally light and equally colorful, which is the property Tableau10/Okabe-Ito actually have. In this figure the six named orthologs went from electric magenta / acid yellow-green / navy / dark crimson to a coherent set (soft blue, warm brown, light blue, green, purple, pink). It stays a hash rather than a list of N curated colors, and that part of the earlier answer still holds: randomColor has no shared state, so there is no allocator handing out the next unused color, and an N-colour palette repeats after N values and collides by the birthday problem long before — six values into a twenty-colour palette collide more often than not. A hue circle does not repeat until 360.
